title: VO lines (TTS-spelled) for aircraft Shorts a1-a3

lines.text: The F thirty-five should have been called the F twenty-four.
Since nineteen sixty-two, American military aircraft names have followed one system.
Under its rules, the next new fighter after the Y F twenty-three should have taken the next number in line: twenty-four.
Instead, the winning demonstrator, the X thirty-five, simply kept its number.
And the F thirty-five is far from the only aircraft name that breaks the rules.
One letter can turn a cargo plane into a gunship.
The C one thirty Hercules is a cargo plane.
Put an A in front, and the A C one thirty is a gunship.
H makes it a rescue aircraft. E, electronic warfare. K, a tanker.
Same airframe. One letter changes the job.
And that's just one of six parts a military aircraft name can have.
For years, people were sure a secret F nineteen stealth fighter existed.
In July nineteen eighty-six, the Air Force sealed off a crash site in Nevada, and the rumors exploded.
The jet that crashed was actually an F one seventeen, still classified at the time.
No real F nineteen has ever been shown to exist.
Even stranger: the F one seventeen got an F for fighter, with no air-to-air mission at all.
